Reviewer #1:

Overall, the question studied in this work is timely, interesting and important. More specifically, although previous modeling studies have been focused on explaining how humans and other animals can learn informative abstract representations at the behavioral level, the underlying neural mechanisms remained poorly understood. Cortese and colleagues performed modeling analyses using a mixture of experts RL that consist of abstract and feature RL models as well as behavioral analyses (analyses of choice in a learning task) to demonstrate that performance of human subjects in a multi-dimensional learning task depends on their adopted level of abstraction. Supporting their modeling and behavioral analyses, authors analyzed fMRI data to demonstrate that the connections between ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), the brain area encoding value signals, and visual cortex (VC) can predict subjects' learning speed, which is an indicator for adoption of abstract representations. Lastly, to demonstrate the causal relationship between VC and adoption of abstract representations, authors used a multivoxel neurofeedback procedure and showed that artificially adding value to features in VC results in an increase in adoption of abstract representations.

Although provided analyses are thorough and results are convincing, further quantitative analyses could be included to strengthen the main claims of the study. More specifically, it is helpful to show that results from fitting the mixture of expert approach is fully consistent with analyses using purely Abstract and/or Feature RL models. Additionally, an analysis of excluded subjects' behavior is missing. This is important, because failure in performing the task could indicate alternative (but unsuccessful) representations adopted by some subjects.

Comments for the authors:

(1.1) Page 6-8 and Figure 2: I could have missed this, but authors don't seem to provide any formal comparison between the goodness-of-fit using the mixture of expert RL model and pure Feature RL or Abstract RL models. For example, a simple Abstract RL model with only the informative features could capture behavior of certain subjects. I asked this because, the mixture of expert RL model contains more parameters than the Feature and Abstract RL models. I wonder when accounting for the extra parameters, would the mixture of expert RL model still provide a better fit? Please clarify.

(1.2) Related to the previous point, if the mixture of expert RL model provides a better fit, how much of the captured variance is related to the Feature RL vs Abstract RL experts (e.g. Figure 3F, G)? Perhaps this could be answered by examining the weight assigned to each type of RL in this model (λ values).

(1.3) Authors don't show the values of responsibility signals in the mixture of expert model. This information, in addition to 'mean expected value', is needed to draw conclusions on the importance of Feature and Abstract RL models.

2) I feel that the decoding analysis can be further improved. For example, do authors see any changes happen as a result of experience in the task? Also, a relevant reference is a study by Oemisch et al., Nat. Comm 2019, in which the prevalence of feature encoding neurons is examined.

3) How did the excluded subjects perform the task? Do they adopt a different strategy and that is why they could not learn fast/accurately enough? For example, did they learn about the value of different features and combine these values to make decisions (as in feature-based RL in Farashahi et al., 2017 or Farashahi et al., 2020, which is different from Feature RL and closer to Abstract RL)? Please comment.

4) Does VC-vmPFC coupling predict the abstraction level? This connection seems to be as important to authors' claims as the discussed relationship between VC-vmPFC coupling and learning speed (Figure 4C).

Reviewer #2:

Cortese and colleagues report two experiments in which human subjects made choices based on cues that had three distinct visual features. Only two of the three visual features were needed to make a correct choice. Hence participants could safely ignore one feature and learn based only on the two relevant features (a process the authors call abstraction). The authors modelled how behaviour and ventromedial prefrontal cortex activity shifted from processing all features to only the two relevant features and sought to elucidate the role of feature valuation in this process. In a second experiment, the authors used a real-time neurofeedback approach to tag visual representations of features and showed how this feature valuation process shapes the feature selection described in Experiment 1.

Past research has investigated the process by which humans and other animals learn to attend relevant features during reinforcement learning (e.g., Niv et al., 2015; Leong et al., 2017). These studies have outlined how reward shapes which features we pay attention to, and how attention shapes how we process reward. While a true account of how the process of "abstraction" might occur is still outstanding in my opinion (see below), this study adds some important insights about this process. A main point is that the authors show changing representations of features directly in vmPFC, which co-occur and interact with values. They also provide insight into the unique roles vmPFC and the hippocampus might have in this process, and how vmPFC value signals interact with sensory areas.

One particularly interesting aspect is this study is the use of neurofeedback to achieve reward-tagging of visual representations. This approach is noteworthy as it does not require to pair reward with the visual features themselves, but rather with the occurrence of neural representations that reflect said features. The behavioural effects of this manipulation on later learning were impressively strong: if the task required to attend features that were tagged with reward, behaviour was guided more strongly by appropriate selective learning; if the task required to ignore the features that were previously tagged with reward, the learning process was unchanged. This suggests that the process of selecting relevant features during learning interacts with a neural mechanism that tracks the values associated with these features. This conclusion is also supported by the fact that the same brain area that tracked the expected values of the stimuli during the task, vmPFC, was modulated by participants' level of feature selection, i.e. abstraction.

One weakness of this study is that the mechanism of abstraction remains unclear. The authors use a mixture of experts architecture of 4 different RL models: one RL model that tries to learn the appropriate action as a function of all visual features of the cues, and 3 models that try to learn based on the possible subsets of only two features.

I have some concerns about this approach. One concern is that the modelling presumes that participants concurrently run all 4 RL models, and continuously decide which one is best. The whole purpose of using a lower dimensional model is that it is more efficient. Permanently using 4 models, including the highest dimensional one, seems to defy the purpose of why the search for a best model was initiated in the first place. Arguably, such a scheme would also not necessarily predict that vmPFC should come to selectively represent only the most relevant features, since the model that requires processing all features needs to be kept up to date. It also does not shed light on how participants could ever truly stop to pay attention to some features, as feature selection is only done by weighting the model with the lowest prediction errors relative to the variance most strongly in the action selection process. In other words: I am unsure if the manuscript presents a reasonable account how representations become transformed. Other models, which do not suffer from these shortcomings, such as a function approximation model, might have added important insights to this study. Ideally, the presented model could also explain another interesting observation made by the authors: that performance improves over blocks, even though the relevant features change. This probably reflects that participants might have learned something more global about the dimensionality of the relevant space, but such a learning process is not accounted for by the authors. On the positive side, while such a concurrent training of 4 models seems computationally inefficient, it is at least data efficient, as each experience is used to update all models at once. And, the mixture of experts approach may be considered a tool to investigate feature selection, rather than a cognitive model. This should be clarified in the manuscript.

Another weakness of the manuscript in my opinion is that the valuation process targeted in the neurofeedback experiment presupposes that visual features are predictive of reward. One important aspect of abstraction, however, is that they may not be, as the same feature could lead to different outcomes, for instance based on unobservable context.

Comments for the authors:

– It would be great to try to model how longer-term knowledge about rewarding features and dimensionality of the task influence performance. How does the change over blocks occur? How do biases, as introduced through the neurofeedback procedure, influence model selection in the mixture of experts approach?

– Figure 5: Could it be that participants are simply better (more correct choices) in the abstract blocks (which presumably are also the later blocks)? If so, wouldn't that mean that the contrast high-low value in vmPFC will necessarily be higher for abstract blocks, but it could reflect performance rather than strategy?

– It would be interesting to see performance separately for CO, CD and OD blocks as well as for 2x2 vs 3x1 blocks. Is there a difference between 2x2 vs 3x1 blocks?

– Please consider avoiding the word "predict" when reporting a regression analyses or other types of non-causal effects.

– I did not follow how the variance over RPEs (v) is calculated. It would be important to clarify that in the manuscript, and indicate how it changes as learning progresses.

Does a small variance imply that all models have similar RPEs? If so, I am not sure the statement that it is related to sharper model selection is the only way to view it. It seems it could also be related to more model similarity.

– Isn't the fact that the relevant AbRL has higher values and learns faster trivial, given the design of the task? Would there have been any possibility that these results would not have come out? If not, I believe all p values should be removed.

– It would be great to add the results from Figure S6 into the main manuscript. The specific different between relevant and irrelevant features seems important

– Decoding: was the cross validation done between runs? If not, if should be done between runs if possible

– Neurofeedback: can you provide more information about how good participants were, and how long the neurofeedback effect was presented in the later task blocks (did it diminish over time?).

Reviewer #3:

The authors of this study aimed to demonstrate that abstract representations occur during the course of learning and clarify the role of the vmPFC in this process. In a novel association learning paradigm it was shown that participants used abstract representations more as the experiment went on, and that these representations resulted in enhanced performance and confidence. Using decoded neurofeedback, (implicit) attention to certain features was reinforced monetarily and this led to these features being used more during the association task. They conclude that top down control (vmPFC control of sensory cortices) guides the use of abstract representations.

The strengths of this paper include an objective, model based assessment of reinforcement learning, a strong and simple experimental paradigm incorporating variable stopping criteria, and the incorporation of decoded neurofeedback to determine if these representations could be covertly reinforced and affect behavior.

The weaknesses include a small sample, the lack of subjective evaluation of strategies/learning, and the omission of neurofeedback learning results.

Overall the authors achieved their aims and the data supports their conclusions.

This work will be of significance to computational psychologists, those who study abstraction and decision making, and those interested in the role of the vmPFC. One exciting implication of this work is that the use of certain features can be reinforced via decoded neurofeedback.

Comments for the authors:

I am not an expert in computational methods, therefore my comments are largely restricted to the neurofeedback study. The neurofeedback task is well designed and the use of relevant and irrelevant features is a nice control condition. That the effects were only observed for relevant blocks and the finding of increased abstraction from the late blocks of the main experiment strengthens their conclusions regarding causality.

While this is not the main focus of the manuscript, a supplement should contain the results of the neurofeedback experiment. Were participants successful at increasing the size of the disc? Was there a correlation between this success and subsequent performance on the association paradigm?

6s of modulation seems short for neurofeedback studies, please justify this short modulation time.

Finally, I am curious as to whether subjects were interviewed regarding the strategies they were using during the association paradigm. Were they aware they were using abstraction?

[Editors' note: further revisions were suggested prior to acceptance, as described below.]

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Value signals guide abstraction during learning" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been evaluated by Michael Frank (Senior Editor) and a Reviewing Editor.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed, as outlined below:

1. Please revise your paper such that a casual reader will not erroneously take away that the MoE model presents a solid account of the data. Right now, the MoE is still mentioned in the abstract and also presented prominently in one of the main figures. You can leave the model in the manuscript if you want, but please further tone down any claims related to it.

2. It would be important to mention that some of the excluded subjects had good overall performance and the distribution of strategies was different among them.

Reviewer #1:

Authors have adequately and thoroughly addressed my concerns and questions. The only remaining concern I have is related to point # 1. Based on the presented results, it seems that MoE model does not provide the best fit of data. However, authors clearly mention and discuss this limitation in the revised manuscript. I have no further comments or concerns.

Reviewer #2:

I thank the authors for their thorough response to our previous concerns. I have two main concerns left:

1. The model comparison seems to refute the MoE model. At the same time, it seems clear that neither the FeRL nor AbRL model alone can truly capture participants behavior, since participants switch from one model to the other during the course of behavior. I think this should be made very clear in the paper, and I wonder how useful including the MoE model is.

My main reason is as follows: the core benefit of the MoE model, its ability to flexibly mix the two strategies, is seemingly not implemented in a way that reflects participants behavior. Would there be any way to improve the MoE models flexibility? The fact that it provides a "proof of concept that an algorithmic solution to arbitrate between representations / strategies exists" alone does not convince me, since the arbitration itself seems to not capture behavior and the pure existence of some algorithm is hardly surprising. In addition, there are the concerns about how realistic the MoE model is, which were raised under point 4.

I am also wondering whether the bad fit of the MoE model reflects how the fits were calculated: within each block, and then averaged (if I understood correctly)? Does that mean there was a new set of parameters per block? Have the authors tried to fit over the entirety of the experiment, using one set of parameters?

Relatedly, I believe that the change between strategies over time should be presented in one of the main figures, as this is an important point (e.g. by putting the rightmost graph from the Figure shown in the point by point response in the main paper).

2. I am also not fully convinced by the explanations about exclusions. The fact that the excluded subjects showed a different distribution of strategies should not serve as a reason for exclusion, since the purpose of the paper is to elucidate, in an unbiased manner, the distribution as it exists in the general population. The reported accuracy also does not seem very low for some participants. To me it seems that including the overall high performing subjects (with e.g. avg % correct > 70%) would provide a more unbiased sample.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work in mice.

claims.source: An attractive view is that valuation may be interpreted as an abstraction in itself. Value could provide a simple and efficient way for the brain to operate on a dimensionless axis.

claims.source: Neuronal encoding of feature-specific value, or choice options, may help the system construct useful representations that can, in turn, inform flexible behavioural strategies (Niv, 2019; Schuck et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Valuation subserves a critical function in constructing abstractions.
claims.source: In summary, this work provides evidence for a function of valuation that exceeds the classic view in decision-making and neuroeconomics. We show that valuation subserves a critical function in constructing abstractions.

claims.claim: Valuation, by generating a common currency across perceptually different stimuli, may be an abstraction in itself, and is tightly linked to the concept of task states in decision-making.

claims.claim: Value is not a simple proxy of a numerical reward signal, but is better understood as a conceptual representation or schema built on-the-fly to respond to a specific behavioural demand.
claims.source: In this context, value is not a simple proxy of a numerical reward signal, but is better understood as a conceptual representation or schema built on-the-fly to respond to a specific behavioural demand.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the study's findings.

claims.claim: Value signals in the brain play an important algorithmic role in development of sophisticated learning strategies.

results.result: Participants (N=33) successfully learned novel association rules in a task where pacman-like characters' fruit preferences were governed by combinations of two out of three visual features. Performance exceeded chance by trial 2, learning speed increased across blocks, and neither block type nor association type systematically affected learning speed.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28 and C31 provide converging behavioral evidence with appropriate statistical tests (t-tests, correlations) and are supported by figures. The experimental design is clearly described, sample size is adequate (N=33), and results show consistent learning patterns with proper controls for confounding variables.

results.result: Participants' self-reported confidence in task performance correlated specifically with learning speed and degree of abstraction, but not with total number of trials or proportion of successes.
results.evaluation: Claims C29, C30, C22, and C42 demonstrate a specific relationship between metacognitive confidence and learning strategy. Statistical tests are appropriate (robust regression, correlation comparisons), and the specificity of the correlation (learning speed but not other metrics) strengthens the interpretation that confidence relates to abstraction ability.

results.result: A mixture-of-experts reinforcement learning model with Feature RL (8 states) and Abstract RL (4 states) algorithms successfully captured participant behavior. Simulations and empirical data showed that the appropriate Abstract RL had highest expected value and responsibility, and RPE variance correlated negatively with learning speed.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C38 describe a computational modeling approach with clear model architecture and validation. The model successfully reproduces key patterns in both simulations and participant data (C36-C37), and the correlation between RPE variance and learning speed (C38, p=0.015) provides quantitative support for the model's psychological validity.

results.result: Participants shifted from Feature RL to Abstract RL strategies over the course of learning. Feature RL was slower and less efficient in simulations, predominated in slow-learning blocks and early sessions, while Abstract RL predominated in fast-learning blocks and late sessions. Degree of abstraction correlated positively with learning speed across participants.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41, C45-C46, C65-C66 provide converging evidence from simulations, block-level analysis, and temporal dynamics. Statistical tests are appropriate (sign tests, robust regression with p<0.001), and the pattern is consistent across multiple analyses. The shift from Feature RL to Abstract RL is demonstrated both within and between participants.

results.result: When considering all blocks regardless of fit, Feature RL showed higher learning rates and greediness compared to Abstract RL.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 report statistically significant differences (p<10^-10 and p<10^-30) with appropriate non-parametric tests. However, the supplementary analyses (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) show this pattern reverses when considering only best-fitting blocks, suggesting these differences may reflect model misspecification rather than true algorithmic differences. The authors acknowledge this complexity in their interpretation.

results.result: The vmPFC showed strong correlation with anticipated value magnitude at stimulus presentation, and this region prioritized and selected latent task elements during abstraction both locally and through connections to visual cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C47, C3, and C4 are supported by fMRI GLM analysis with appropriate whole-brain correction (p(FWE)<0.05) and are consistent with prior literature on vmPFC function in value computation. The finding is illustrated in Figure 4A and represents a key neural signature of the valuation process.

results.result: Functional connectivity between visual cortex and vmPFC was higher on high-value trials compared to low-value trials, and the strength of this VC-vmPFC coupling correlated positively with learning speed across participants.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 and C69 are supported by psychophysiological interaction (PPI) analysis and between-subject correlation (p=0.016). The specificity of the VC-vmPFC connection (only this pathway showed value-dependent modulation) and its behavioral relevance provide strong support for the proposed mechanism of abstraction through value-based sensory feature integration.

results.result: vmPFC activity distinguished between Feature RL and Abstract RL learning strategies, showing higher engagement during Abstract RL, while hippocampal activity remained similar across both strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 and C76 are supported by linear mixed effects model analysis with appropriate post-hoc comparisons (vmPFC: p(FDR)=0.009; HPC: p(FDR)=0.54). The differential engagement of vmPFC but not HPC provides evidence for region-specific roles in abstraction, though the interpretation would benefit from additional control analyses.

results.result: Multivoxel pattern analysis revealed that feature classification accuracy was significantly higher during Abstract RL trials compared to Feature RL trials in both HPC and vmPFC, with the opposite (non-significant) pattern in visual cortex. This difference was significantly larger in HPC/vmPFC compared to VC.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are supported by appropriate MVPA with cross-validation and statistical testing (t-tests, LMEM). The control analysis with equated trial numbers (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) confirms the finding is not due to unequal sample sizes. The pattern suggests feature information is actively represented in higher-order regions during abstract learning, not just read out from sensory cortex.

results.result: Searchlight MVPA showed significant reduction in feature decoding accuracy in OFC, ACC, vmPFC, and dorsolateral PFC when a feature was irrelevant to the rule compared to when it was relevant.
results.evaluation: Claims C56 and C77 are supported by whole-brain searchlight analysis with appropriate cluster correction (p(fpr)<0.01). The finding extends the ROI-based results and demonstrates that prefrontal regions selectively represent task-relevant features, consistent with their proposed role in goal-dependent abstraction.

results.result: In a neurofeedback experiment (N=22), artificially adding value to a neural representation of a task-relevant feature in visual cortex resulted in increased use of Abstract RL strategies specifically when that feature was relevant to the block rule, but not when it was irrelevant.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C62 and C92 provide causal evidence for the role of feature valuation in abstraction. The specificity of the effect (relevant vs. irrelevant blocks) is demonstrated with appropriate statistical tests (binomial test p=1.37×10^-7, Wilcoxon signed rank test p=0.015, permutation test p<0.001). The unconscious nature of decoded neurofeedback strengthens the interpretation that the effect operates at the sensory representation level.

results.result: Participants who were more successful at neurofeedback training showed larger increases in abstraction in the subsequent behavioral test compared to their initial level.
results.evaluation: Claim C63 is supported by correlation analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) showing a dose-response relationship between neurofeedback success and behavioral change. This strengthens the causal interpretation of the neurofeedback manipulation by demonstrating that the magnitude of neural manipulation predicts the magnitude of behavioral effect.

results.result: Value signals guide the construction and selection of abstract representations during learning. The vmPFC uses valuation of low-level sensory features to forge abstract representations through goal-dependent processes implemented as top-down control of sensory cortices.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C6, C14, C21, C23, C105, and C109 represent the main theoretical conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the convergence of behavioral modeling (showing value-based strategy selection), neuroimaging (showing vmPFC value signals and VC-vmPFC connectivity), MVPA (showing feature representations in prefrontal regions), and causal neurofeedback evidence. The integration across multiple methods and levels of analysis provides strong support for this novel interpretation of value's role in abstraction.

results.result: In this task, learning faster requires using Abstract RL rather than Feature RL. This builds on prior work showing that efficient decision-making depends on higher-order representations, and extends it by showing that feature valuation supports formation of abstract representations for learning computations.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68, C70-C71 connect the current findings to theoretical frameworks in reinforcement learning and decision-making. C67 is directly supported by the task structure and simulation results. C68 and C70 appropriately cite prior work. C71 represents a reasonable extension of the findings, though it is somewhat inferential.

results.result: Excluded participants (N=11) had overall lower performance than included participants, though some had comparable accuracy ratios.
results.evaluation: Claim C32 is supported by statistical comparison (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Wilcoxon test p=0.006). This validates the exclusion criteria and demonstrates that excluded participants represent a distinct group with genuine learning difficulties rather than arbitrary exclusions.

results.result: Activity in insular and dorsal prefrontal cortices increased under conditions of low expected value, consistent with error monitoring and processing.
results.evaluation: Claim C48 is supported by fMRI analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and is consistent with cited prior work on error monitoring. This represents an expected control finding that validates the value manipulation but is not central to the main hypotheses about abstraction.

results.result: Block rules were encoded in multivoxel activity patterns within the OFC/DLPFC circuitry.
results.evaluation: Claim C79 is supported by searchlight MVPA (Figure 5E) and is consistent with cited prior work on rule representation in prefrontal cortex. This finding demonstrates that abstract task rules are explicitly represented in prefrontal regions, supporting the broader framework of the study.

results.result: The study demonstrates that abstraction emerges during the course of learning in two fMRI experiments where human volunteers learned novel association rules based on simple visual features.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C20 accurately describe the overall experimental approach. The emergence of abstraction during learning is demonstrated by the temporal analyses (C45-C46) showing shifts from Feature RL to Abstract RL over time. This represents one of the two stated aims of the study and is well-supported by the data.

results.result: The vmPFC and HPC have distinct but complementary roles in abstraction: the HPC stores and updates conceptual memories while the vmPFC creates new concepts through valuation-driven channeling of sensory features to higher-order areas. Task states are continuously reconstructed rather than maintained in a fixed location, enabling robust decisions based on relevant, up-to-date information.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 and C80-C81 represent theoretical interpretations that go beyond the direct evidence. While C72-C74 are supported by citations to prior work, C75 and C80-C81 are inferences from the current data. The finding that HPC activity doesn't distinguish learning strategies (C52) is consistent with this framework, but the study doesn't directly test the proposed division of labor or the dynamic reconstruction hypothesis. These claims require additional experimental validation.

results.result: The study examined abstraction at the lowest level (simple visual features rather than complex objects), but the authors speculate that the same valuation-based mechanism should generalize to higher levels of abstraction with different sensory modalities coupling to vmPFC depending on task demands.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 accurately characterize the study's scope. Claims C86-C91 are explicitly speculative predictions about generalization. While these are reasonable hypotheses based on the current findings and prior literature (C88 is partially supported by the PPI results), they require direct experimental testing. The authors appropriately acknowledge these as speculations requiring future work.

results.result: It remains unclear whether value affects abstraction by enabling more efficient construction of abstract representations or by improving selection among existing internal models. Parallel prefrontal-basal ganglia circuits may track different levels of abstraction in hierarchical fashion.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C96 identify important open questions and speculative mechanisms. The current study cannot distinguish between construction and selection mechanisms (C95), and the hierarchical circuit hypothesis (C96) is speculative though supported by citations. These represent appropriate acknowledgments of the study's limitations and directions for future research.

results.result: The results argue against top-down attention as the sole driver of Abstract RL. Instead, attention is likely an effector of abstraction and valuation processes, as evidenced by the unconscious operation of decoded neurofeedback and the pattern of feature decodability across regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 address an important alternative explanation. The argument is supported by the pattern of MVPA results (no marked increase in VC decodability during Abstract RL, C54) and the neurofeedback manipulation (which operates unconsciously, C98). However, the distinction between attention as driver vs. effector is somewhat conceptual, and the evidence doesn't completely rule out attentional contributions. The evaluation is reasonable but not definitive.

results.result: Valuation may itself be an abstraction, providing a dimensionless common currency that indexes task states and behavioral strategies. This interpretation reconciles findings in decision-making and memory literature, positioning value as a conceptual representation built on-the-fly rather than a simple numerical reward signal.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 cite prior work appropriately. Claims C102-C103, C106, and C108 represent theoretical interpretations that are conceptually appealing and consistent with the data, but go beyond what the current experiments directly demonstrate. The idea that value is itself an abstraction is philosophically interesting but would require additional experimental evidence to establish. These represent important theoretical contributions but remain somewhat speculative.

results.result: Recent work in mice shows that value governs functional remapping in sensory cortex through direct OFC projections carrying RPE information and by modulating neuronal gain to irrelevant stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 accurately cite recent rodent work (Banerjee et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020) that provides mechanistic support for the current findings in humans. These citations appropriately contextualize the neurofeedback results and suggest potential neural mechanisms, though cross-species generalization should be interpreted cautiously.

results.result: The introduction establishes theoretical background: abstraction is the ability to organize information beyond immediate sensory reality; classic RL algorithms collapse in complex problems but abstraction to lower-dimensional manifolds enables efficient behavior; the vmPFC computes value, forms schemas, and is well-positioned to extract latent task information; and task goals determine what is valuable.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C13 and C15-C19 provide appropriate background from prior literature with proper citations. These claims establish the theoretical motivation for the study and are well-supported by the cited work. They represent accurate characterizations of the relevant prior literature rather than novel findings.

results.result: Prefrontal regions construct goal-dependent task states and abstract rules from relevant sensory information. HPC neurons continuously generate representations of alternative future trajectories and replay past cognitive trajectories.
results.evaluation: Claims C78, C82-C83 appropriately cite prior work to contextualize the current findings. These represent established findings from the literature that provide theoretical framework for interpreting the current results, particularly the dynamic reconstruction hypothesis.

results.result: This work reconciles apparently disconnected findings in decision-making and memory literature on the role of the vmPFC.
